evidence.quote: David Sacks shared some fascinating numbers on All-In:
- SpaceX: ~$50B in monetization per GW, with roughly a 1-year payback.
- CoreWeave: ~$20B per GW, with roughly a 2.5-year payback.
These are estimates, but the difference is enormous.
A big reason is how the two companies structure their contracts.

CoreWeave relies heavily on long-term commitments to finance its infrastructure. SpaceX has the balance sheet and access to capital to operate with much shorter contracts, giving it exposure to today’s significantly higher compute pricing.
Now consider SpaceX is targeting ~13 GW of operational compute capacity by the end of 2027.

items.summary: Succinct披露SP1 V6原生Rust验证器高危漏洞：6.0.0至6.8.0反序列化未校验张量长度与维度，恶意证明可被接受。链上Groth16/Plonk路径不受影响，自建原生验证器需升至6.8.1。

evidence.quote: Earlier this month, Succinct published a high-severity advisory for SP1 V6, and the press picked it up last Friday.
It affects the sp1_hypercube, sp1_prover and sp1_sdk crates from 6.0.0 through 6.8.0.
During deserialization, nothing checked that the storage length matched the product of the dimensions.
According to the advisory, that was enough for the verifier to accept a proof of an invalid execution.
It only applies to Core and Compressed proofs sent straight to the native Rust verifier.
Groth16 and Plonk wrapped proofs have fixed shapes, so the onchain Solidity verifier path was unaffected.
If you run your own native verifier and accept proofs from provers you don't control, upgrade to 6.8.1 or later.

evidence.quote: The loan I spent most time on is DDTL 5.5, a $2.6bn facility CoreWeave closed in August. It's a delayed-draw loan, so CoreWeave draws it down as it buys GPUs, which it rents out to customers on contracts. The loan matures in September 2031 and the contracts average about three years, so around 2029 CoreWeave will need new customers for those GPUs.

The lenders are well protected. They hold a guarantee from the parent, CoreWeave Inc., and the GPUs and contracts as collateral, and they test the loan every time a contract is renewed or replaced. The new contract has to be with a qualifying customer, and the payments still due under CoreWeave's contracts have to add up to at least 2.40 times what's left on
If CoreWeave fails, it has five business days to pay down enough of the loan to pass. On top of that, the lenders charged SOFR + 550, or 5.5 points over the benchmark rate.

So CoreWeave is left with a possible cash payment around 2029, sized by the gap between what's left on the loan and what the new contracts support. How big it gets depends on what two- and three-year contracts for that GPU generation pay in 2029, and on whether CoreWeave can find enough qualifying customers willing to sign for that long. Exchanges have started listing GPU rental futures this year. @CMEGroup's H100 and B200 contracts were set to start trading on NYMEX on 5 October, each covering a month of rent on one GPU and settling against a @Silicon_Data index. @ICE_Markets has announced similar futures with @OrnnExchange, another index provider, covering H100, H200, B200 and RTX 5090.
